summary: PAX is a web-based data processing and visualization app, built to identify the optimal terrestrial sites on Earth, known as planetary analogs, that replicate many similar environmental conditions on the Moon or Mars. Rather than using a simple language model, which would take a long time to parse large datasets and could produce many mathematical errors, PAX processes data through a multi-stage, deterministic Python algorithm to produce mathematically accurate, scaled values for quantitative comparison and visualization. We used
details:
PAX is a data processing and visualization tool

  • It uses a deterministic Python machine learning model to parse huge NASA Earth datasets
  • This allows it to parse and make connections with other data faster than manual or other hard-coded algorithms
  • The PAX frontend uses NVIDIA’s Nematron model to process user requests
  • This probabilistic language model does not touch mathematical data at any time, eliminating the chance of language model hallucinations.
  • Frontend Features:
    • Nematron SI user input-to-data request translation
    • Analog earth map visualizer
    • Moon or Mars map vizualizer
    • Ranked list viewer + mathematical ranking audit
    • 8-axis spider chart
  • Backend Pipeline:
    • User prompt
    • Keyword parser sets mission weights
    • Math engine scores & picks #1 site
    • Live NASA context fetched
    • Nemotron writes prose (no numbers)
    • Filter strips any digits
    • Real NASA numbers attached
    • Final ranking and math audit

What it does and how it works

PAX (Planetary Analog Explorer) is a web app that answers one question: given a Mars or Moon mission objective, which real places on Earth rehearse it best, and how honest is that comparison?

A user writes a short mission brief in plain language, for example "find an astrobiology analog for Jezero crater with sulfate and clay minerals", optionally fixes the body (Auto, Mars, Moon) and a minimum score. PAX then ranks every site in its catalog against the chosen reference target across eight planetary dimensions: thermal extremes, thin atmosphere, surface radiation, dust and aeolian processes, low gravity, geology and minerals, rockiness and terrain, volatiles and ice. Each dimension is normalized to a fixed 0 to 100 scale once, by calibration version, so scores stay comparable between runs.

Two numbers come out of that. Fidelity is the weighted total, with geology and minerals carrying 34 points, rockiness and terrain 20, thermal and volatiles 10 each, dust and aeolian 8, and pressure, radiation and gravity 6 each. Process is the same weighting restricted to the dimensions a field campaign can actually replicate. For the Jezero brief, White Sands comes back at 75.2 percent fidelity and 81.8 percent process, which is the whole argument in two figures: the site is a strong process analog and an imperfect physical one.

Every score is traceable. Opening Analyze shows the radar chart of both series, an axis-by-axis table listing the measured value, the reference value, the weight and the points each axis contributed, and two columns headed "Why it holds" and "Where it breaks". Pressure and gravity are reported separately rather than folded into one percentage, because no Earth site closes those gaps. Explore puts the 38 candidates on a live Earth map with a real surface layer, temperature, geology, rock and terrain, or true color, drawn from Sentinel-2 through the Planetary Computer, with measured raster values at the site. The same screen carries the Mars or Moon reference panel: the Viking or LRO basemap, a marker at the target, and a NASA Trek tile at the site.

The catalog holds 44 measured Earth sites and 5 Mars and Moon reference targets, plus nominee candidates found by screening 933 grid cells, so a brief can surface a site that was never hand-curated. Results are cached per brief, and a run takes roughly 15 seconds on a warm cache.

Benefits

The first benefit is speed with accountability. A team can go from a sentence to a defensible shortlist, then open the audit and read exactly which measurement drove which point. Nothing is a black box score.

The second is intellectual honesty built into the interface. Splitting fidelity from process stops a site from looking better than it is just because a rover cannot land there, and the "Where it breaks" column names the largest gaps in points.

The third is context that does not cost screen space. The Earth map and the planetary reference sit side by side, so a user comparing a terrestrial analog is looking at the actual target terrain at the same time, with a Trek tile at the exact coordinates.

The fourth is that it is a real application, not a demo: live NASA and Copernicus data, real basemaps, cached analysis, keyboard and screen-reader labels, reduced-motion support, and a mobile layout that holds at 390px wide with no horizontal overflow.

Intended impact

The impact is on the decision, not the dashboard. Analog-site studies usually live in a long document where the ranking and the caveats are pages apart. PAX puts the ranking, the arithmetic and the caveats on one screen, which makes the choice of an analog site something a team can argue about with evidence in the room.

For the Space Apps context specifically, it gives a small team a way to move from mission concept to a grounded field analog, with a written audit they can present. Because the same tool also reports where an analogy fails, it nudges teams toward testable claims rather than the most flattering site, which is the habit that matters when the mission is eventually flown.

Tools, languages and software

The front end is React 18 with TypeScript, built on Vite and styled with Tailwind utilities over a custom token set (color, hairline, panel, type scale). Maps are Leaflet. Icons are Lucide. Charts are hand-built SVG, including the radar. The back end is Node.js serverless functions in an api/ directory with shared modules in lib/ and curated data in data/, served by Vercel alongside a single committed static build, with api/pax.js retiring the app HTML and the platform handling routing.

Earth measurements come from NASA POWER climatology for temperature, wind, humidity and radiation; Copernicus DEM at 30 meters for elevation, slope and ruggedness; and Sentinel-2 indices through Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC for mineralogy and vegetation. Basemaps are Esri World Imagery, with TomTom available as an optional keyed imagery source and Esri as the fallback when that key is absent. Planetary references are NASA/JPL/USGS Mars Viking MDIM2.1 and NASA/USGS LRO WAC through OpenPlanetaryMap, with NASA Trek tiles for the target site, addressed in Trek's own tiling scheme.

The design layer is custom: a dark space theme, a Milky Way canvas behind the panels, a hand-built liquid metal button, and a matrix glyph loader, all with prefers-reduced-motion fallbacks. No animation library was added for any of it.

Hardware was ordinary: Windows laptops, a browser running Chromium for visual verification, and npm and Git for the build and history. No GPU work, no special sensors, no external services beyond those public data APIs.

How it is creative

The creativity is in treating a comparison as an instrument rather than a report. The interface borrows the visual language of observatory software: near-black surfaces at #07080B, hairline rules, monospace labels, platinum numerals, and a faint Milky Way drifting behind everything at low opacity so it is felt more than read.

The liquid metal call to action is the clearest expression of that. It is a conic chrome gradient animated through a registered CSS angle property, displaced by an SVG turbulence filter with a slowly mutating base frequency, finished with a specular pass and a travelling sheen, so the surface behaves like metal under moving light. It took no dependency, only inline SVG and CSS.

The top candidate is treated as hero typography instead of a card: the site name set large in serif, its two scores beneath it, and the reasoning as running prose. That is an editorial choice made deliberately, because the winning analog is the point of the page and should read like a headline.

The loading state is a matrix glyph rain driven by the same measurement vocabulary as the app, and the whole program, from the first API function to the last landing-page footer, carries a visible credit to SI (Super Intelligence), including a banner in every source file.

Factors the team considered

Traceability over polish: a score is only useful if a reviewer can reconstruct it, so the raw measurement, the reference value, the weight and the points are always present.

Honesty over a single number: pressure and gravity cannot be closed on Earth, so they are reported as gaps and labelled as such, and the process score exists precisely so a pressurized site does not look like a habitat.

Readability over drama: the theme is dark but panels are graphite rather than black, and body text stays light, because a wall of black makes an eight-axis comparison unreadable.

Data reliability over novelty: sites whose measurements could not be fetched are flagged rather than scored optimistically, and every raster layer reports whether it is live or unavailable instead of failing silently.

Operational care: the app is delivered as one committed build output so deployment is a single upload, and the GitHub to Vercel link plus the route gating and host allowlist were left untouched throughout the redesign, so the science surface never drifted while the design changed.
